topic_tag: voles in a grass strip beside a rail line
passage: Beside a rail line, a strip of uncut grass runs twelve miles across plowed farmland past small woodlots, and meadow voles live in both the strip and the woodlots. Two decades of trapping suggest that the strip has served as the voles' ______. Young voles pushed out of crowded woodlots each spring settle in the strip's seed-heavy grass within a few hundred yards of where they entered, and owls hunt it from the line's poles. Within a month, tags of over half the voles marked there turn up in pellets beneath the poles, while those that wander back to a woodlot breed there the next spring.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: "Cemetery" fits: young voles settle in the strip, and owls hunting from the poles kill more than half of them there within a month, so the strip is where the voles die. "Corridor" fails because the voles stop within a few hundred yards of where they enter and are killed there within weeks, so they do not pass along it. "Cage" fails because voles can wander back to a woodlot, so the strip does not hold them in. "Cafeteria" fails because, although the voles feed on its seed, over half of them are killed there by owls within a month, so what the strip mainly does to them is kill them, not feed them.

topic_tag: a coral outcrop in a lagoon
passage: A lone coral outcrop the size of a car rises from the sand of a shallow lagoon, a quarter mile inside its ring of reef. By day, snappers and groupers from the outer reef gather near it in loose groups and take turns hanging head-down beside it, gill covers flared, while shrimp living in its crevices crawl over them and into their mouths. Each fish swims back to the reef within minutes of its turn. On a nearby reef where divers removed every shrimp, groupers now spend hours rubbing their flanks against the sand. Divers who have logged its visitors since 1985 call the outcrop the lagoon's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: "Clinic" fits: fish take turns hanging still while the outcrop's shrimp crawl over them and into their mouths, and where the shrimp were removed groupers rub themselves against the sand, which shows the shrimp had been ridding them of something that irritates them; the outcrop is where reef fish go to be cleaned. "Canteen" fails because the visitors hang motionless with mouths open while shrimp work on them; the visitors are being tended, not eating. "Bedroom" fails because the visits are by day and end within minutes. "Ballroom" fails because the groups are of mixed species, each fish hanging alone in its turn, with no courtship.

topic_tag: a dam and the river below it
passage: In 1960 a dam was built across a mountain river, holding back a reservoir three hundred feet deep. Twenty years of surveys show that the dam has ______ the river below it. Its turbines draw water from near the reservoir's floor and pass it through at an even rate, day and night, and each May the snowmelt flood pours over the spillway and rolls the gravel bars below. The stretch below the dam, once thick with bass, now holds almost none; trout spawn instead on gravel bars lying as deep under water as before 1960, and the bass have retreated to reaches thirty miles downstream.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: "Chilled" fits: the turbines release water from the bottom of a deep reservoir, and below the dam trout have replaced bass, which now live only thirty miles downstream, so the river below has turned cold. "Bled" fails because the gravel bars lie as deep under water as before 1960, so the river below carries as much water as ever; the bass left for another reason. "Churned" fails because the release is even day and night, and the only surge is the river's own snowmelt flood spilling over in May, not anything the turbines do. "Clogged" fails because that flood still rolls the gravel bars every year, so silt and plants cannot settle and choke the channel.

topic_tag: a neutral island port in wartime
passage: In the second year of the war, the northern alliance ______ the island's only port. Before the war the port had shipped wool to buyers on both sides of the strait. That spring the island's wool, until then half of all the wool the alliance imported, disappeared from the alliance's markets within a month, while freighters bound for neutral countries loaded more of it at the port than ever, emptying the waterfront sheds as fast as they filled. The harbormaster, appointed as always by the island's council, reported the busiest year in the port's history.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: "Boycotted" fits: the wool was being shipped from the port in record amounts, yet it disappeared from the alliance's markets, so the alliance had stopped buying from the port. "Blockaded" fails because freighters loaded more wool than ever and the port had its busiest year, so ships came and went freely. "Bombarded" fails because the waterfront sheds were filling and emptying with record cargoes, so the waterfront was working. "Annexed" fails because the island's council still appointed the harbormaster.

topic_tag: the fate of an empty town church
passage: In 1951 the last congregation left a stone church that had stood at the center of a river town since 1720. Engineers that winter found its walls sound and its tower true, and a merchant offered the council a good price for the ground it stood on. By the next spring that ground was a parking lot for the new market hall, and the church's stones, broken small, had been spread as the bed of the road to the new bridge. The town's minutes record that in 1952 the council ______ the church.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: "Bulldozed" fits: within a year the church's ground was a parking lot and its stones were broken up and laid under a road, so the council had it knocked down. "Condemned" fails because condemning is a declaration that a building is unfit, and the council went much further, tearing down a church its engineers had found sound and breaking up its stones. "Crated" fails because stones broken small and spread under a road were never packed to be rebuilt. "Commandeered" fails because the council made no use of the church building; it cleared it away and used the ground.

topic_tag: small birds on an island flowering tree, netting experiment
passage: On one island a single species of small bird drinks at the flowers of a native tree and roosts in its crown. For three years an ecologist netted the birds off some branches and compared them with open ones. Under the nets the flowers dropped whole, unbitten by insects. Caterpillars chewed netted and open leaves alike while the birds fed head-down in the blossoms, and nearly every flower a bird had probed swelled into a hard green fruit that fell unopened beneath the tree, where the island's few seedlings come up. In those three years, the birds ______ the tree.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Flowers the birds could not reach dropped whole without setting fruit, while nearly every flower a bird had probed set fruit, so the birds "pollinated" the tree. "Patrolled" fails because the birds spent their visits head-down in the blossoms and caterpillars chewed netted and open leaves alike, so the birds kept no insects off. "Propagated" fails because the fruit falls unopened beneath the tree, where the seedlings come up, so the birds carry no seed anywhere. "Parasitized" fails because the nectar the birds drink is repaid: without them the tree sets no fruit at all.

topic_tag: nesting falcons and a city square's pigeons
passage: When a pair of peregrine falcons began nesting on a cathedral spire in 1996, birdwatchers began counting the pigeons in the square below each winter and banding their chicks each spring. Over the following decade, the falcons ______ the flock. Its pairs nested on their old ledges, the lowest a few yards below the falcons. Most bands picked up under the falcons' ledge came from birds over five years old or crippled by the string that tangles city pigeons' feet, and with fewer mouths at the crumbs, far more chicks lived to a second spring, so by 2006 the winter count stood where it had in 1996.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The falcons took mostly old birds and birds crippled by string, and with fewer mouths at the crumbs more young survived, refilling the flock to its old count, so the falcons "rejuvenated" the flock, replacing old and lame birds with young ones. "Reduced" fails because the surviving young brought the count back to its 1996 level. "Redistributed" fails because the pairs kept to their old ledges. "Rattled" fails because the lowest pairs nested a few yards below the falcons, which unsettled birds would not do.

topic_tag: a poet's first collection, 1851
passage: In 1851 a young poet paid a printer in her city to issue three hundred copies of her first collection, on terms that gave her a share of every copy sold. Within months a celebrated actress began reciting the poems, naming the poet each night, in sold-out halls across the country, and cheap editions appeared in every city she played. Each carried her printer's license on its back page, her share of every copy reached her within the quarter, and the city papers had already named two of the poems among the season's best. Within two years, her poems had been ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: A celebrated actress recited the poems in sold-out halls across the country and cheap editions followed her from city to city, so her poems had been "popularized": carried to a wide public. "Pirated" fails because each cheap edition carried her printer's license and paid her share of every copy, so none was printed without leave. "Plagiarized" fails because the actress named the poet each night. "Panned" fails because the city papers had named two of the poems among the season's best.

topic_tag: an occupying army and a port city's museum, 1797
passage: In 1797 an occupying army entered a port city whose museum held some four hundred paintings and bronzes, many of them carried off from neighboring towns by the city's own fleet a century earlier. Its officers crated the bronzes and the largest canvases, listed each against a number, and left the council a copy signed by the commander. The bronzes went to the army's foundry and came out as cannon, the canvases were hung in the commander's headquarters, and the council's offer to buy them back was turned down. Within a year, the army had ______ the museum's collection.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The officers took the bronzes and big canvases under a signed list, melted the bronzes into cannon, hung the canvases in the commander's headquarters, and refused to sell them back, so the army had "requisitioned" the collection: seized it officially for its own use. "Ransacked" fails because the pieces were crated, numbered and signed for, not rifled. "Ransomed" fails because the council offered to buy the pieces back and the army refused. "Repatriated" fails because the pieces went to the army's foundry and headquarters, not to the towns they had come from.

topic_tag: an ancient clay tablet listing barley
passage: A clay tablet dug from the ruins of an ancient river city lists barley in nine lines, each giving an amount, a word or two, and a number, and a seal has been rolled across its back. The words run barley from the river fields, dates from the southern groves, water, then barley again, sprouted, and then crushed, and the numbers are days, three beside the sprouting and one beside the crushing. A second column repeats every amount exactly doubled, the seal is the temple brewer's, and the tablet lay among the brewery's jars. Scholars now read the tablet as its owner's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The lines move through ingredients and then through stages of the same barley, sprouted and then crushed, with days of waiting beside the stages, and a second column doubles every amount, all under the brewer's seal, so the tablet is the brewer's "recipe": quantities and steps for a brew in two batch sizes. "Roadmap" fails because the days sit beside stages of one batch of barley, so the places named are only where the ingredients come from, not stops on a route. "Receipt" fails because a column that restates every amount at exactly twice the size sets out quantities to use, not goods someone acknowledged receiving, and the seal is the brewer's own. "Payroll" fails because no line names a person.

topic_tag: a moorland village's spring walk
passage: Every spring until 1914, the people of one moorland village walked out at dawn in ribboned hats across six miles of common where their ponies grazed, coming home by dusk from the boundary stone beside a spring at the edge of the neighboring parish. Folklorists who recorded the walk in 1900 called it the village's yearly ______. At the stone each family drank from the spring and tied a ribbon from its hats to the thorn above, already hung with ribbons of other springs, then walked home between the grazing ponies with water for anyone too ill to come; the neighboring parish came to the same spring a week later.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Each family drank from the spring, left a ribbon on a thorn hung with ribbons from earlier years, and carried its water home to the sick, so the walk was a "pilgrimage": a journey to a place held to be holy, made in devotion. "Roundup" fails because they walked home between the grazing ponies, leaving them where they were. "Pageant" fails because the ribbons were left on the thorn as offerings, and the water went to the sick, so the hats served a devotion, not a show. "Raid" fails because the neighboring parish visited the same spring on its own day, so the spring was shared, not taken from them.

topic_tag: a store at a mountain gold camp, 1859
passage: In 1859 a merchant built a log store at a mountain gold camp, the only building there with a stove, an iron safe and a shelf of bottles, and his ledger survives. One historian of the camp called the store, in those years, the camp's ______. Beside each watch, pistol or fiddle left in the safe, the ledger enters a sum paid to its owner, most of it spent on flour and powder. The same things reappear months later, most marked as taken back for that sum and a tenth more, the rest priced on the shelf beside the whiskey bottles, in a stove room that had no chairs.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Miners left watches, pistols and fiddles in the safe and received sums of money against them, then took them back for the sum plus a tenth or saw them priced for sale, so the store was the camp's "pawnshop": a lender against pledged goods. "Repository" fails because the goods were not simply kept for their owners: money was paid out against them, and unredeemed ones were put up for sale. "Pharmacy" fails because the bottles on the shelf held whiskey. "Parlor" fails because the stove room had no chairs, so it was where business was done, not where the camp sat together.

topic_tag: a logging road over thirty years
passage: A two-lane road laid across a valley floor in 1960 carried loaded logging trucks for thirty years, and surveyors checked it each fall against stakes along its shoulders. Each July its asphalt softened in the heat, and the trucks, keeping to the same wheel tracks on the narrow lanes, pressed it a little lower every summer, most on the long climb, where they crawled. By then rain stood for days after every storm in two long lines up the climb, while at the stop sign below it, where the trucks braked hard, the asphalt lay as flat as the day it was laid. By 1990, its surface had been ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Softened asphalt was pressed a little lower each summer under trucks that always used the same wheel tracks, and by 1990 rain pooled for days in two long lines up the climb, so the surface had been "rutted": worn into grooves along the wheel paths. "Rippled" fails because folds come from braking trucks shoving asphalt forward, and at the stop sign, where they braked hard, the asphalt lay flat. "Raised" fails because the asphalt was pressed lower, not lifted. "Ruptured" fails because the rain stood in the grooves for days without draining away, so the asphalt beneath it held unbroken.

topic_tag: a merchant shipwreck after two centuries
passage: A wooden brig loaded with roofing slates sank in thirty feet of water off a sandy coast that storms strike every winter. Two centuries on the seabed had ______ the ship, divers reported after surveying it. The hull lies where it settled on open sand that the current sweeps clean each tide, and its outline, keel to rails, can still be traced from above. A plank the divers lifted weighed less than a loaf and crumbled in their hands. Its surface was pale and smooth except for holes no wider than a pencil lead, and slates that slid through the sagging planks lie crusted with barnacles around the hull.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: "Gnawed" fits: a plank that looks smooth outside, apart from pencil-lead holes, weighs almost nothing and crumbles, so creatures have eaten the wood away from within. "Entombed" fails because the current sweeps the sand off the hull every tide, leaving it exposed. "Encrusted" fails because the barnacles are on the spilled slates, while the plank's own surface came up pale and smooth. "Dismantled" fails because the hull's outline can still be traced from keel to rails; the planks are sagging where they are, eaten hollow, not broken apart and scattered.

topic_tag: an estate's brick orchard wall
passage: In 1760 a riverside landowner built a brick wall twelve feet high and a quarter mile long beside his orchard, near a village of thatched cottages. It runs along the orchard's northern edge, open at both ends, and the river runs past the orchard's southern edge, with the village on its far bank. Peaches trained on the wall's sunny face set fruit in springs when frost blackens every other blossom, and the bricks there stay warm to the hand at midnight. A fire in 1791 burned the village to the ground and never crossed the water. Estate letters of the next fifty years treat the wall as the orchard's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: "Hearth" fits: the bricks on the wall's sunny face hold heat into the night, and the peaches trained against them set fruit in springs when frost kills the blossom everywhere else, so the wall is the orchard's source of warmth. "Fence" fails because the wall runs along one edge only and is open at both ends, so it closes nothing in or out. "Dike" fails because the river runs past the orchard's southern edge while the wall stands on its northern edge, with the trees between them, so the wall cannot hold the river off the orchard. "Firebreak" fails because the village lies across the river, and when it burned, the fire stopped at the water; it never came near the wall on the orchard's far side.

topic_tag: a salt mine and a city's art museum
passage: For a decade the old salt mine served the nearby city's art museum as its ______. Its chambers lie six hundred feet down, where the air stays cool and dry all year, reached by a single lift. The museum sent down the paintings it had struck from its catalog, water-stained copies and works no buyer would take, and miners leaned them in rows along the walls of a worked-out chamber, which was then bricked up. The museum's inventory marks each of them destroyed, and the chamber has not been opened since.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: "Dump" fits: the museum sent down works it had struck from its catalog and could not even sell, its inventory marks them destroyed, and the chamber was walled up and never reopened, so the mine was where it got rid of them. "Depository" fails because a depository keeps things for their owner to retrieve; these works had been struck from the catalog, so the museum no longer counted them as its own, and its inventory now marks them destroyed, so they were put away for good rather than held for later. "Hospital" fails because the water-stained copies were leaned against the walls and bricked in, with no one ever working on them. "Gallery" fails because, although the paintings were set out in rows along the walls, the chamber was bricked up at once and has stayed shut, so no one ever saw them.

topic_tag: beavers in a dry mountain valley
passage: For thirty years beavers have lived on a creek in a dry mountain valley; the creek in the next valley has none. Black mud studded with the creek's own pebbles lies heaped in ridges along the banks, and a pole pushed into each pool finds bottom three feet deeper than in the next valley's creek. The beavers live in burrows in the banks and build no dams, and the creek's surface stands where old survey stakes put it. A hydrologist who has studied both valleys concludes that the beavers have ______ theirs. Aspens shade both banks, and by midsummer the grass browns with the rest of both valleys.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: "Dredged" fits: mud full of the creek's own pebbles lies heaped on the banks, and the pools are three feet deeper than in the creek next door, so the beavers have scooped out their creek's bed. "Flooded" fails because they build no dams and the creek's surface stands where old survey stakes put it; the extra depth is below the water, not over the land. "Deforested" fails because aspens still shade both banks. "Greened" fails because by midsummer its grass browns with the rest of both valleys.

topic_tag: a river flood on a farm field
passage: One spring the river rose over a farmer's lowest field and stood there nine days. The field is loose sand, and the water, clear from a reservoir upstream, sank into it as fast as the river refilled it. The sand was still wet when the corn went in on schedule, fertilized like the higher field, and by June dry wind was lifting it off the rows. That corn came up pale and short beside the dark green rows above. Walking the field in late summer, the county's soil scientist said that the flood had ______ it. The higher field, never flooded, gave its usual yield.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Nine days of water sank steadily down through loose sand, and corn given the same fertilizer as the higher field came up pale and short, so the flood had "leached" the field, carrying its nutrients down out of the roots' reach. "Manured" fails because equal fertilizer produced weaker corn on the flooded field than on the dry one, so the flood took food from the soil rather than adding it. "Mulched" fails because the water ran clear from a reservoir, carrying no litter to lay down, and by June the wind was lifting the bare sand off the rows, which no covered field allows. "Mired" fails because, wet as the sand still was, the water had been draining down through it and the corn went in on schedule.

topic_tag: a salt marsh and the bay it drains into
passage: Twice daily the bay's tide floods a salt marsh at a farm creek's mouth, then drains it through one channel. A team spent two years sampling that channel. Each winter ice cuts the marsh grass to stubble, and spring ebbs carry the shredded stems into the cove below. The ebb also left with as much of the creek's farm fertilizer as had come in, and as muddy. Cove shrimp grow fastest within a mile of the channel, where the stems settle. The team's report calls the marsh the bay's ______. As those stems rot on the cove's floor in late summer, its deep water runs short of oxygen.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The ebbs carry the marsh's shredded grass into the cove, and the shrimp grow fastest just where those stems settle, so the marsh is the bay's "kitchen": the place where its animals' food is made. "Kidney" fails because the water left with all the creek's fertilizer, so the marsh removed none of that waste. "Net" fails because the marsh sends material out rather than catching it: the water left as brown with mud as it came, now carrying the stems too. "Lung" fails because the cove below it runs short of oxygen as the marsh's stems rot there, so what the marsh sends the bay uses oxygen up rather than supplying it.

topic_tag: desert dunes and an oasis village
passage: For two centuries after 1700, the dunes of a desert basin pressed against a walled oasis village of mud-brick houses and date palms. Through the 1700s they spread across the basin's rim, and the old caravan road now lies forty feet beneath them; the only way in runs over their crests, a three-day walk. The village itself lies in a still hollow below dunes taller than its palms, its doorways opening onto the lanes at the height their builders set. Its families kept every house and date garden, selling dates only to the rare walker who came through. In those two centuries, the sand had ______ the village.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The dunes buried the caravan road forty feet deep, so the village could be reached only by a three-day walk over their crests, while its families went on living in a hollow among them: the sand had "imprisoned" it, shutting it in. "Lifted" fails because, though the way in now runs forty feet above the old road, the village's own doorways still open at their builders' height, so the sand rose around the village, not under it. "Nibbled" fails because the families kept every house and date garden; the dunes took the basin around the village, not pieces of the village. "Lashed" fails because the village lies in a still hollow below dunes taller than its palms, sheltered from the wind that would drive sand against it.

topic_tag: a park on an old rail yard
passage: A forty-acre rail yard became a park, with a highway to its north and, to its south, row houses and apartment towers the yard had divided for a century. Its lawns slope open to the highway, its ball fields and weekend market in the middle. Gate counts found as many visitors as other parks its size draw, nearly all walking from the row houses and towers in equal numbers on the same evenings and staying two hours. By decade's end a third of tower families had row-house friends, once one in twenty. A study of the park's first decade called it the district's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Residents of the two neighborhoods the yard divided came in equal numbers on the same evenings and stayed two hours, and friendships between them rose from one tower family in twenty to one in three, so the park is the district's "mixer," where the two communities come together. "Magnet" fails because the park draws no more visitors than the city's other parks of its size; what sets it apart is not how many it pulls in but the friendships formed among those who come. "Junction" fails because a junction is where ways meet and cross, and these visitors stay two hours at the fields and market; what the park changed is how the people in it relate, which is mixing. "Muffler" fails because the lawns slope open to the highway, leaving nothing to absorb its noise.

topic_tag: a wartime government and its newspapers
passage: During a two-year war in the 1870s, one small country's government changed how it dealt with the country's four daily newspapers. Their editors joined a press committee that met weekly with the war ministry, and the four dailies ran its recruiting appeals and casualty lists free of charge. The man who had written the papers' prewar peace columns now wrote their weekly appeals to enlist, and no ministry official saw a page before it ran. The founding families paid for the added pages out of profits that climbed with wartime sales. One historian's account of those years says the government ______ the press. Two of those editors later wrote memoirs.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The editors met weekly with the war ministry, ran its recruiting appeals and casualty lists free, and the papers' own peace writer turned to urging readers to enlist, so the government "mobilized" the press, enlisting it in the war effort. "Muzzled" fails because the peace columns stopped when their own writer changed sides, and no official saw a page before it ran, so the press was recruited, not silenced. "Nationalized" fails because the founding families still owned the papers and paid for the added pages. "Impoverished" fails because those families paid out of profits that climbed with wartime sales.

topic_tag: sandbar at a river-mouth port
passage: A sandbar lies across the river mouth below the old port, twelve feet under water at high tide and bare at low tide. Harbor records from the 1800s show the bar serving as the port's ______ for most of a century. Ships crossed it on every high tide, often several abreast, steering without a pilot along a straight channel marked by public buoys, and tied up at the town's piers to unload. In winter gales the ocean swells broke in a white line along the bar, and fishing boats moored at those piers rode out storms that wrecked boats anchored along the open coast.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The swells broke along the bar while boats moored behind it at the piers survived storms that wrecked boats on the open coast, so the bar sheltered the harbor from the sea: a "seawall." A "tollbooth" is a point where everyone passing must pay, but ships steered over without a pilot along publicly buoyed water, so crossing cost them nothing. A "turnstile" admits traffic one at a time, but ships crossed several abreast on every high tide. A "wharf" is where cargo is loaded and unloaded, but the ships crossed the bar and unloaded at the town's piers.

topic_tag: drought in a pine forest
passage: From 1952 to 1957 almost no rain fell on a pine forest in the southern hills, where foresters measured every tree yearly until 1975. Every tree tagged in 1952 still stood in 1975, and the needles grown in the dry summers stayed on the branches their usual three years. Once the rains returned, the pines' growth rings stayed narrow for a decade, and bark beetles, which a healthy pine drowns in resin, bored into one tree in five, large and small alike, and lived in them for years. The foresters' final report concluded that the dry years had ______ the forest.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: No tree was lost, yet afterward the pines grew slowly for a decade and let in beetles that a healthy pine drowns in resin, so the drought left them weakened: it "sapped" the forest. "Winnowed" means sifted out the weaker part, but every tagged tree survived, and the beetles settled in large and small trees alike, so nothing was sorted out. "Scorched" means burned or browned, but the needles grown in the dry summers lasted their usual three years. "Toppled" means brought down, but every tree tagged in 1952 still stood in 1975.

topic_tag: stones in a steep river's bed
passage: Two geologists measured the stones of a steep river running eight miles from granite and sandstone cliffs to the sea. Their report argued that the river had ______ those stones, and its photographs set out the case. Sieved, the bed held oven-sized boulders at the cliffs, fist-sized cobbles midway, and pea gravel at the sea. Painted stones turned up, flood by flood, wherever the bed held stones their own size. Below a spring that runs orange, the stones are orange too, the color running clear through any stone cracked open. At the mouth, in water gray with grit, broken pebbles still fit back together edge to edge.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Each stretch of the river held stones of nearly one size, and painted stones traveled with each flood to wherever the bed held stones their own size, so the river had separated its stones by size along its course: it had "sorted" them. "Stacked" means set one on another, but the painted stones moved on with every flood. "Stained" means colored from outside, and the spring does run orange, but the orange runs clear through any stone cracked open, so it is the rock's own color. "Sanded" means worn down by grit, and the river at the mouth carries grit, but broken pebbles there still fit back together edge to edge.

topic_tag: valley glacier above farming villages
passage: A glacier fills the head of a high valley whose river runs past farming villages to the plain. It melts only in sunshine, and its meltwater runs straight down bare rock, so the river at the villages rises each summer evening and falls before dawn. The mills start their wheels at the evening rise. Paintings show its front at one rock ledge in 1790, the frozen 1810s and the hot 1860s. The ditches draw on springs.
